title: Sketches and Balloons
summary: Leonardo da Vinci filled notebooks with drawings of flying machines, but never flew. Then, in 1783, two French paper-makers filled a giant bag with hot air, and a sheep, a duck and a rooster went for a ride. A few weeks later, two men floated over Paris, the first people ever to fly freely!

sections.heading: The Man Who Watched Birds
paragraphs: Imagine walking through the streets of Florence or Milan in the late 1400s and passing a man standing completely still, staring up at the sky, scribbling in a small notebook. He watches a kite-bird circle, then a pigeon flap away, then a swift dart past. He sketches the angle of each wing, writes a note, sketches again. That man is Leonardo da Vinci, and he is doing something that almost nobody before him had done so carefully: studying flight like a scientist.

Leonardo, who lived from 1452 to 1519, is famous today as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. But painting was only one part of his life. He was also an engineer, an architect, an anatomist who studied how bodies are built, and a tireless inventor. He filled thousands of notebook pages with drawings and ideas about water, weapons, machines, plants, the human body and, again and again, flight.

Leonardo wrote most of his notes in mirror writing, from right to left, so that you need a mirror to read them easily. He was left-handed, and writing backwards may simply have been more comfortable and less smudgy for him. Whatever the reason, it makes his notebooks look mysterious and has helped make them famous.

From the 1480s onward he made over a hundred drawings about flying. He studied how birds tilt their wings to turn, how they spread their tail feathers to brake, and how they use rising air to soar without flapping. He also studied bats, whose wings are made of a thin skin stretched over long finger bones. Leonardo liked bat wings as a model because, unlike a bird's wing, air cannot leak through gaps between feathers.

In one of his notebooks he wrote that a man with wings that were large enough and properly attached might learn to overcome the resistance of the air and rise up. He also believed that air pushes back against a moving object just as much as the object pushes against the air. That was a sharp observation. More than 150 years later, Isaac Newton would turn this kind of idea into his famous third law of motion: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. It is still one of the keys to understanding how wings work, as you will learn in Part 9.

sections.heading: Flapping Machines, Air Screws and a Notebook About Birds
paragraphs: Leonardo's most famous flying-machine drawings are of ornithopters. The word comes from Greek words meaning 'bird' and 'wing', and it means a machine that flies by flapping its wings. In some of his designs, the pilot lies flat on his stomach on a wooden frame. His feet push pedals and his hands pull levers, and through ropes and pulleys these movements make two huge bat-like wings flap up and down. In other designs the pilot stands upright inside the machine like a person climbing a ladder.

These drawings are clever and beautiful, but they share a fatal flaw: they still depend on human muscle to flap the wings. Leonardo himself seems to have realised over the years that a human being is too heavy, and too weak, to fly with flapping wings. In his later notes he paid more attention to gliding, the way large birds ride on the wind with still wings. He sketched a fixed-wing glider design, and modern builders have found that gliders based on his ideas can fly with today's light materials.

One of his most famous sketches is what is often called the 'aerial screw' or 'helical air screw'. It looks like a giant spiral of linen stretched over a frame, sitting on a round platform. The idea was that if the spiral were spun quickly, it would screw itself up into the air, a bit like a screw twisting into wood. People often call it the ancestor of the helicopter. But it would not have worked. Human muscles could not spin it fast enough, and even if they could, the platform would have spun in the opposite direction. Real helicopters solve that problem with a small tail rotor or two rotors spinning opposite ways.

Leonardo also drew a parachute: a pyramid-shaped tent of sealed linen held open by a wooden frame, with a person hanging below. He wrote that with such a device a man could jump from any great height without injury. Was he right? In the year 2000, a British skydiver named Adrian Nicholas built a version from wood, canvas and rope, the kind of materials Leonardo could have used, and floated down with it from a hot-air balloon over South Africa. It worked, though he released it and finished his descent with a modern parachute because the heavy wooden pyramid would have been dangerous to land with.

Here is the important point for historians: there is no reliable evidence that Leonardo ever built and flew any of his flying machines. A popular legend says that he, or one of his pupils, tried to fly from Monte Ceceri, a hill near Florence, around 1505, and crashed. But no notebook or letter confirms it, and many historians think the story was invented later. Leonardo's flying machines lived on paper.

And for a long time, they stayed hidden on paper. After Leonardo's death in 1519, his notebooks were scattered, sold and lost. Some ended up in private collections or royal libraries. His ideas about flight were not widely known until the late 1700s and 1800s, long after other inventors had moved on. So, sadly, his careful studies did not directly help the people who finally learned to fly.

The most complete record of Leonardo's thinking about flight is a small notebook called the Codex on the Flight of Birds. A codex is simply an old handwritten book with pages bound together. This one dates to about 1505 and is surprisingly small: just 18 sheets of paper, each about 21 by 15 centimetres, about the size of a school exercise book.

Inside, Leonardo explains how birds fly, how they balance and how they deal with wind. He noticed something that later aircraft designers had to learn all over again: the point where a bird's weight is centred is not always the same point where the air pushes up on its wings. Getting those two points in the right relationship is what makes a flying thing stable or wobbly. He described how a bird shifts its wings and tail to keep balanced, rather like a tightrope walker adjusting with a pole.

The codex also includes ideas for flying machines, notes on gravity and weight, and even sketches that have nothing to do with flight. In the margin of one page there is a faint drawing in red chalk that some researchers believe could be a self-portrait of Leonardo as a younger man, though not everyone agrees.

Today the Codex on the Flight of Birds is kept at the Royal Library in Turin, Italy. It is so precious that it rarely travels. In 2013, it was lent for 40 days to the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C., where it was displayed in the same building as the 1903 Wright Flyer, the first successful powered airplane. Visitors could see, in one museum, both an early dream of flight and its fulfilment four hundred years later.

sections.heading: Borelli Does the Math
paragraphs: Even after Leonardo, people kept trying to fly by flapping. If a person only had better wings, the reasoning went, they could surely flap their way into the sky. In the 1600s, an Italian scientist finally put numbers on the problem and showed why this was hopeless.

His name was Giovanni Alfonso Borelli. He was born in Naples in 1608 and died in Rome in 1679. Borelli was a mathematician and physicist who became fascinated by how living bodies move. He is often called the father of biomechanics, the science that studies bodies as if they were machines made of levers, ropes and pulleys. He looked at bones as levers and muscles as the ropes that pull them, and he used geometry and mathematics to work out how much force muscles must produce for walking, running, jumping, swimming and flying.

His great book was called De Motu Animalium, which is Latin for On the Movement of Animals. Borelli died before it was printed, and it was published in two volumes, the first in 1680 and the second in 1681. His patron, Queen Christina of Sweden, who was living in Rome, helped pay for it, and the book was dedicated to her.

In the part about flight, Borelli compared birds with humans. A bird's chest muscles, which pull its wings down, are huge for its size and make up a large share of its body weight. A human's chest and arm muscles are tiny in comparison with our heavy bodies. Borelli concluded that human muscles are far too weak to flap wings fast and hard enough to lift a person, no matter how well the wings are made. It was simply not possible for a person to fly like a bird using his own strength.

This was a disappointing conclusion for dreamers, but it was a big step forward. Instead of just trying and crashing, Borelli used measurement and reasoning to say why something would not work. That is how science saves lives and time. His work suggested that if humans were ever going to fly, they would need a completely different approach. Some people decided the answer was not to fly like a bird at all, but to float like a cloud.

sections.heading: The Paper-Makers of Annonay
paragraphs: Our story now jumps to the small French town of Annonay, about 70 kilometres south of Lyon, in the 1780s. Here lived the Montgolfier family, who ran a successful paper-making business. Two of the sixteen Montgolfier children would change history: Joseph-Michel, born in 1740, and Jacques-Étienne, born in 1745.

The brothers were very different. Joseph was a dreamer, full of ideas, but not very good at running a business. Étienne had trained as an architect in Paris and was practical and organised; he came home to manage the family paper mill and brought in new paper-making techniques. Together, one dreaming and one building, they made a great team.

How did they get the idea for a balloon? One story says Joseph noticed that clothes drying over a fire billowed and puffed upward. Another says that in November 1782, while he was in the city of Avignon, Joseph sat watching a fire and thinking about a famous fortress, Gibraltar, which the French and Spanish armies were trying to capture. He wondered whether the same force that carried sparks and smoke upward could carry soldiers over the walls.

Joseph made a small box of very thin wood covered with taffeta, a crisp silk fabric, about the size of a small cupboard. He lit some paper underneath it. The box rose up and bumped against the ceiling. He wrote excitedly to Étienne, and the two began building bigger and bigger models. In December 1782 they tested a much larger one, and it floated nearly 3 kilometres before coming down.

The brothers believed the secret was a special gas in the smoke, which they even called 'Montgolfier gas'. So they preferred smoky fires of wet straw and wool. In fact, they were wrong about the smoke. What really lifted their balloons was simply hot air. When air is heated, its tiny particles move faster and spread further apart, so a bag of hot air weighs less than the same-sized bag of cool air around it. The cooler, heavier air pushes underneath and floats the balloon up, the same way water pushes a cork to the surface. They had the right result for the wrong reason, which happens surprisingly often in the history of science.

On 4 June 1783, the brothers gave their first public demonstration in the market square of Annonay, in front of local officials and townspeople. Their balloon was made of sackcloth lined with paper, held about 790 cubic metres of air, and was put together from separate pieces held by about 1,800 buttons. The crowd watched a fire being lit beneath it. The great bag swelled, strained against the ropes, and then, when it was released, rose high into the sky. It stayed up for about 10 minutes and came down roughly 2 kilometres away. Estimates of how high it climbed vary a lot, from about 1,000 to 2,000 metres. News of the flying bag raced to Paris.

sections.heading: A Sheep, a Duck and a Rooster at Versailles
paragraphs: Paris was electrified. The Academy of Sciences invited the Montgolfiers to the capital, and King Louis XVI wanted to see a balloon for himself. Étienne went to Paris and teamed up with Jean-Baptiste Réveillon, a successful wallpaper manufacturer. Together they built a splendid balloon of taffeta, coated with alum to make it less likely to catch fire, and painted sky blue with golden decorations. It was a flying work of art.

Nobody knew whether a living creature could survive high up in the air. Would the air be breathable? Would the cold be deadly? It is said that the king suggested sending up two condemned prisoners. Instead the inventors chose animals for the first test with passengers.

On 19 September 1783, in the courtyard of the royal palace of Versailles, an enormous crowd gathered, including King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette. Into a wicker basket under the balloon went three passengers: a sheep, a duck and a rooster. The sheep was given the name Montauciel, which means 'climb to the sky'. The choice was clever. A sheep was thought to be similar to humans in size and body. A duck was used to flying high, so if it was harmed, the problem was probably the balloon, not the altitude. A rooster was a bird that does not fly high, so it was somewhere in between.

The balloon rose into the sky, drifted for about 8 minutes, travelled roughly 3 kilometres and landed in a wood. It climbed to about 500 metres. When people rushed to the landing site, they found the animals alive. The rooster seemed to have a slightly hurt wing, probably because the sheep had stepped on it or kicked it, not because of the flight. The experiment showed that living creatures could survive a trip into the sky. The way was open for people.

sections.heading: Two Men Floating Over Paris
paragraphs: For the first human flights, the Montgolfiers built an even bigger balloon, about 23 metres tall and 15 metres wide, with a gallery, a kind of round balcony, where passengers could stand. At the bottom, in the middle, hung an iron fire basket. Passengers had to keep feeding it straw to keep the air hot.

Before trying a free flight, they did tethered tests, with the balloon tied to the ground by long ropes. In October 1783, Étienne Montgolfier himself rose a short way into the air on a rope from the Réveillon workshop yard in Paris, and so did a young scientist named Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier, who rose to the end of his tether, about 25 metres up.

Pilâtre de Rozier was a chemistry and physics teacher who had opened his own museum of science in Paris. He was bold and enthusiastic, and he argued that the honour of being the first person to fly should go to someone eager and educated, not to a prisoner. He was joined by an army officer, François Laurent, the Marquis d'Arlandes.

On 21 November 1783, at the Château de la Muette, on the western edge of Paris near the Bois de Boulogne, the great balloon was filled with hot air. In the early afternoon the ropes were released, and for the first time in history human beings rose freely into the sky with nothing holding them to the ground.

Picture the view. Below them spread the rooftops of Paris, the river Seine, church towers and crowds of tiny people looking up. The balloon drifted across the city at perhaps 900 metres high. But it was not a peaceful ride. The two men had to keep feeding the fire. At one point sparks burned holes in the fabric, and they had to put out small fires with wet sponges, and by some accounts with Pilâtre's coat. D'Arlandes later wrote a lively account describing the noises and alarms of the trip.

After about 25 minutes, having travelled roughly 9 kilometres, they came down safely at the Butte-aux-Cailles, which was then just outside the city. They had made the first free flight by human beings in history. The famous American scientist and diplomat Benjamin Franklin, who was living in France at the time, was among those who followed these experiments closely.

It is worth being clear about what this was. It was a real flight, but it was not an airplane. A balloon is lighter than air: it floats because it is less dense than the air around it, like a bubble rising in water. An airplane is heavier than air and must create lift by moving fast through the air. The first true airplane flight was still 120 years in the future.

sections.heading: Hydrogen Balloons and the English Channel
paragraphs: At exactly the same time, another French scientist was working on a different kind of balloon. Jacques Charles, a physicist, knew about a gas discovered by the English scientist Henry Cavendish in 1766: hydrogen, which Cavendish had called 'inflammable air'. Hydrogen is the lightest gas there is, much lighter than hot air, so it could lift far more weight with a smaller balloon.

The challenge was to make enough hydrogen and keep it from leaking. Charles worked with two brothers, Anne-Jean and Nicolas-Louis Robert, who had found a way to coat silk with rubber dissolved in a liquid, making it nearly airtight. To produce the hydrogen, they poured sulfuric acid onto scrap iron. This made huge amounts of gas, but it was slow, messy and expensive.

On 27 August 1783, they launched a small unmanned hydrogen balloon from the Champ de Mars in Paris, where the Eiffel Tower stands today. It flew for about 45 minutes and came down about 21 kilometres away near the village of Gonesse. The villagers there had never seen anything like it. Frightened, they attacked the strange object with pitchforks and tore it to pieces. Benjamin Franklin was in the crowd at the launch. According to a well-known story, when someone asked him what use a balloon could possibly be, he replied: 'What is the use of a newborn baby?' He meant that new inventions start small and grow up into something important.

Then, on 1 December 1783, just ten days after the first hot-air flight with people, Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert took off from the Tuileries Garden in central Paris in a hydrogen balloon. Reports say a crowd of around 400,000 people came to watch, perhaps half the population of Paris. Charles's balloon had many features that balloons still use today: a net over the top to spread the weight, a basket hanging below, a valve to let gas out to come down, and bags of sand as ballast that could be thrown out to go up. They flew for about 2 hours and travelled about 36 kilometres before landing at Nesles-la-Vallée. Then Charles took off again alone, without Robert's weight, and shot up to about 3,000 metres. His ears hurt and it was bitterly cold, so he let out some hydrogen and came down. He never flew again.

Soon people wanted to fly farther. Jean-Pierre Blanchard, a French balloonist who had once tried to steer balloons with flapping oars and paddles, decided to cross the English Channel, the stretch of sea between England and France. On 7 January 1785, he took off from Dover Castle in England with an American doctor named John Jeffries, who helped pay for the trip. Over the cold grey sea the balloon kept sinking. According to accounts of the flight, the men threw out almost everything to stay up, including their equipment and even some of their clothes. After about two and a half hours, they reached the French coast and came down in a forest near Guînes. They were the first people to cross the Channel by air. A stone column was later put up near the landing place.

Ballooning had dangers too. In June 1785, Pilâtre de Rozier, the first person to fly, tried to cross the Channel from France to England in a new kind of balloon that combined a hot-air balloon with a hydrogen balloon. Shortly after take-off, the balloon came down near Wimereux on the French coast, and both Pilâtre de Rozier and his companion, Pierre Romain, were killed. They are thought to be the first people to lose their lives in an air accident. It was a sad reminder that flying needed great care.

Blanchard went on to make the first balloon flight in North America, on 9 January 1793, from the yard of a prison in Philadelphia. President George Washington was there to watch, and the balloon landed across the river in New Jersey.

sections.heading: Why Balloons Were Not the Answer
paragraphs: Within a few years of 1783, balloons were everywhere. They drew huge crowds, inspired fashions, songs and even balloon-shaped furniture. Scientists carried thermometers and barometers aloft to study the atmosphere. During the French Revolution, the French army set up special balloon units to watch enemy soldiers from above, and decades later balloons were used for observation in the American Civil War.

But balloons had one huge problem. A balloon floats inside the air like a cork in a stream, so it goes wherever the wind takes it. A balloonist can go up and down by heating air, letting out gas or dropping ballast, and sometimes find winds blowing in different directions at different heights. But a balloon cannot really be steered against the wind. Blanchard's oars and flappers made almost no difference. Imagine trying to row a hot-air balloon to your school: if the wind blew the other way, you would end up miles off course.

Balloons were also enormous for the little weight they could carry, slow, fragile and at the mercy of storms. Inventors later added engines and propellers to long, cigar-shaped balloons, creating airships, which could be steered. But airships were huge, expensive and slow.

So the old dream remained. Birds do not drift with the wind; they go where they want, even into the wind. To do that, a flying machine would probably have to be heavier than air and hold itself up by moving through the air, like a bird with fixed wings or a kite on a string. Borelli had shown that human muscles could not flap wings. Leonardo's drawings were mostly hidden away. What was needed was someone who could think about flying in a completely new way.

That person was already alive. In 1783, when the first balloons rose over Paris, he was a boy of about ten in England. Around 1799, this English country gentleman took a small silver disc and scratched onto it a picture of a flying machine. It had a fixed wing, a body, a tail and paddles to push it forward. It looked surprisingly like an airplane, more than a hundred years before the first airplane flew. His name was George Cayley, and in Part 3 you will see how he cracked the code of flight.

deepDive: Balloons work by buoyancy, described by Archimedes' principle: any object in a fluid is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Air at about 20 degrees Celsius near sea level has a density of roughly 1.2 kilograms per cubic metre. Heat it to about 100 degrees Celsius and, at the same pressure, its density drops to about 0.95 kilograms per cubic metre, because density is inversely proportional to absolute temperature (293 K versus 373 K). Each cubic metre of hot air therefore gives only about 0.25 kilograms of lift. That is why the 1783 Montgolfier balloons were so enormous: a balloon of 1,700 cubic metres might give a few hundred kilograms of lift, much of it used up by the heavy envelope, gallery, fire basket and fuel. Hydrogen, with a density of only about 0.09 kilograms per cubic metre, gives roughly 1.1 kilograms of lift per cubic metre, about four times as much as hot air. That explains why Charles's 380 cubic metre balloon could carry two people while the Montgolfier balloon carrying two people needed several times the volume. Charles's interest in gases also led to the law that bears his name: at constant pressure, a gas's volume grows in proportion to its absolute temperature. He never published it; Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac did in 1802 and credited Charles's earlier unpublished work. Historians also debate earlier claims. In 1709 the Portuguese-Brazilian priest Bartolomeu de Gusmão demonstrated a small hot-air device to the king of Portugal, and some Portuguese-speaking writers call him the true inventor of the balloon, but evidence is thin and most aviation historians credit the Montgolfiers with the first practical hot-air balloon. In 1670, the Italian Jesuit Francesco Lana de Terzi proposed an airship lifted by four copper spheres emptied of air, but thin spheres would have been crushed by air pressure. As for Leonardo, scholars stress that his flight studies, while brilliant, had almost no influence on later pioneers because his notebooks were unknown for centuries. Borelli's 1680 analysis of muscle power was more influential: it helped persuade later thinkers, including Cayley, to separate the job of lift from the job of propulsion.
funFact: The first passengers ever carried by a hot-air balloon, in September 1783 at Versailles, were a sheep named Montauciel, a duck and a rooster, and all three landed alive.
